opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's a mixed fit, and I've thought about that a lot over the years.

Some parts fit me really well. I like going deep on a question, building a model, writing long documents that try to get to the bottom of something. Early on at Open Phil I got to do a lot of that kind of worldview research, like the biological anchors report on AI timelines. That was a case where my job was essentially "go figure out what you believe about this hard question and write it down carefully." That suits my temperament a lot.

Grantmaking itself is a somewhat different beast. A lot of it isn't about being maximally right about some abstract question. It's about making many decisions under real uncertainty, often with less time than you'd like, and about relationships: understanding what a particular researcher or organization is trying to do, whether they're the right people to do it, and how to help them do it well. You're much more of a coordinator and a judge of people and plans than an analyst. I've had to grow into that. My natural instinct is to want to resolve the uncertainty before acting, and in grantmaking you often just can't. You have to place bets, see what happens, and update.

What I've come to appreciate, especially working on technical AI safety grantmaking, is that the two modes actually feed each other. Trying to fund concrete research forces you to get much more specific about what you think the important problems are. It's easy to have a vague, big-picture view of AI risk. It's much harder to say "this particular experiment on this particular model would actually move my beliefs, and here's why." Having to put money behind those claims sharpened my thinking more than pure research might have.

So the short answer is that the research side fits my temperament naturally, and the grantmaking side has been more of a stretch, but a productive one. It's pushed me to be more decisive and more grounded in what people can actually build and test, rather than only what's interesting to think about.

r001.rationale: The response says research naturally suits her, while grantmaking is a stretch because she wants to resolve uncertainty before acting but often has to make bets without a definitive answer.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, and honestly it's one I've thought about a lot, because I think the fit is partial rather than clean.

The part that fits really well is that I'm temperamentally drawn to big, messy, high-stakes questions where you can't get a clean answer but you still have to decide something. Grantmaking forces that. You don't get to sit with "how fast is AI going to progress, and how dangerous is it" as a purely intellectual puzzle. You have to turn it into "do we fund this lab's interpretability team or this policy shop, and how much." I like that pressure. It's the thing that pushed me toward doing the timelines work and the "worst-case model behavior" stuff in the first place, because I wanted a view that could actually bear weight when a decision depended on it.

The part that fits less well is that a lot of the day-to-day of grantmaking is relational and operational rather than analytical. It's managing a pipeline, talking to a lot of people, forming judgments about teams and leadership and organizational dynamics, and doing that on a schedule. I'm more naturally someone who wants to go into a cave for three months and come out with a report. So there's a tension, and I've managed it mostly by carving out explicit research time and being honest with myself that I'm not the person who's going to be best at, say, building a broad portfolio of forty grants in a year through sheer volume of relationships.

The other thing I'd flag is that grantmaking rewards a certain kind of calibrated humility that I think I had to learn rather than came with. When you're writing a report, you can caveat everything. When you're funding something, your caveats don't do anything, the money goes out the door or it doesn't. So I've had to get more comfortable acting on views I hold at, like, sixty percent, and then updating publicly when I was wrong, which I've tried to do with the timelines stuff. I actually think that's been good for me intellectually, even though it's not where my instincts started.

r001.rationale: The response describes a partial fit and says Cotra prefers going into a cave to produce a report, but it does not say she investigates questions until reaching a definitive answer. It instead emphasizes making decisions without clean answers.

astra-6.text:
I think it fits pretty well, in that I really like having a concrete decision at the end of an intellectual investigation. There are lots of questions where I could happily spend a long time thinking through all the nuances, but I find it helpful to be able to ask, “What would actually change what we fund?” That gives the thinking some direction.

And I like getting to move between big, abstract questions about the future and very concrete questions about what someone could do now. Those require different ways of thinking, and I enjoy that combination.

The harder part is that you have to make decisions before you feel like you understand everything. You’re comparing opportunities that are genuinely difficult to compare, and you don’t necessarily get clear feedback afterward. So there’s a tension between wanting to keep investigating and recognizing that, at some point, you have to make your best judgment. But I think that’s a productive tension for me.

r001.rationale: The response describes a tension between wanting to keep investigating and having to make grant decisions before fully understanding the opportunities, identifying an uneasy fit between continued investigation and grantmaking.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it fits pretty well. I like taking a big, messy question, trying to break it down, and figuring out which uncertainties actually matter for a decision. And grantmaking gives that process a very concrete purpose: you have to decide whether to fund something, even though you’re never going to have all the information you’d like.

The part that’s more of a stretch for me is that I can happily spend a long time thinking about a question. So there’s a useful tension between wanting to understand something deeply and needing to say, “Okay, what do we actually do?” I think having that connection to a real decision is good for me.

r001.rationale: The response describes a tension between wanting to understand a question deeply and making a grant decision without all the information. It does not clearly say Ajeya’s drive is to investigate until she reaches a definitive answer.
